diagrams.title: OpenStack: simple boundary overview
diagrams.caption: The simplest presentation view: cloud services run in Pods, libvirt still owns host-cgroup guests, and OVN owns their fabric. Text labels identify what the qrab target keeps, replaces and still needs to finish. Arrows are selected control and guest paths, not a complete service call graph.

diagrams.title: qrab: simple target boundary overview
diagrams.caption: The matching presentation view: Kubernetes owns intent, manager owns QEMU inside its container, and a separate anchor gives each NIC a Cilium identity. The shared platform remains. The overview omits detailed storage/control paths and does not claim all replacement capabilities are complete.

diagrams.title: Migration: simple ownership and stream overview
diagrams.caption: A slide-sized view of VM-state, switch-control and node-conntrack boundaries. Source and target managers represent the same immutable VM; node peers have separate node identities. This omits detailed preparation, route forwarding and cleanup; use the sequence/state diagrams for those.

diagrams.title: Storage: simple control and I/O overview
diagrams.caption: A slide-sized split of scoped provisioning and native guest disk I/O. The root helper owns exports/fences; guest block bytes flow directly through QEMU libiscsi. UEFI/vTPM state remains a separate filesystem volume.

diagrams.title: OpenStack: current deployment boundaries
diagrams.caption: The operator-supplied model: Kubernetes hosts the services; libvirt still owns host-cgroup VMs, and OVN owns guest networking. Cilium and FRR are shared platform foundations.

diagrams.title: qrab: target ownership on the current source
diagrams.caption: Kubernetes owns declarative intent; a manager owns QEMU inside its container, and separate NIC anchors connect guests to Cilium. Storage provisioning and guest I/O are different paths.

diagrams.title: Where OpenStack responsibilities move
diagrams.caption: Replace the service control planes, preserve their required work. Image and volume replacements are constrained foundations with remaining scope.

diagrams.title: Processes, containers and privileged helpers
diagrams.caption: QEMU and swtpm are manager children. Restricted VM/anchor Pods rely on separate privileged device and network helpers; privilege does not disappear.

diagrams.title: Containerized libvirt versus a container-owned VM
diagrams.caption: The OpenStack side is the supplied deployment model. The qrab side shows direct QEMU supervision within the manager container cgroup.

diagrams.title: Two network planes become one Cilium fabric
diagrams.caption: Reusing Cilium removes the OVN guest fabric while preserving distinct endpoint identities for management and every guest NIC.

diagrams.title: Control messages and guest payloads
diagrams.caption: Kubernetes config and private QMP control the VM. Packets and block I/O do not pass through the operator; VM migration has its own payload tunnel.

diagrams.title: Five identity questions with different answers
diagrams.caption: A human subject, an action grant, a service SVID, a guest workload and a CHAP export are different scopes. None is a universal credential.

diagrams.title: A VM launch crosses explicit owners
diagrams.caption: A conditional storage owner gate protects native disks. The kubelet starts the manager; the manager requests local NIC descriptors and publishes no API updates itself.

diagrams.title: Power off is not Pod deletion
diagrams.caption: The manager survives an in-place power off. A fresh power-on cycle starts new QEMU/swtpm children while retaining the intended VM identity.

diagrams.title: A guest packet through its NIC identity
diagrams.caption: Kernel TAP/vhost queues carry packets through the anchor netns. netd grants descriptors and plumbs resources; its Unix control stream does not relay packets.

diagrams.title: Storage provisioning versus disk I/O
diagrams.caption: Delegated API authorization reaches narrow root storage verbs. QEMU independently opens its CHAP-authorized LIO session for guest block I/O.

diagrams.title: From verified source to a sealed clone origin
diagrams.caption: The image controller orchestrates token-free inspect/write Jobs and separately authorized storage stages. Retirement prevents new clones; it does not erase existing guest disks.

diagrams.title: Disk export ownership and hard fencing
diagrams.caption: Conceptual lifecycle, not a verbatim enumeration of API phases. Fencing is complete only after backend barriers; irreversible destruction has separate authority.

diagrams.title: Migration moves more than RAM
diagrams.caption: VM state, switchover control, node conntrack and forwarded guest packets are separate streams. Shared guest disk blocks are not copied through the manager tunnel.

diagrams.title: Prepare, transfer, switch and adopt
diagrams.caption: Target anchors are prepared as fenced standbys. The final pause transfers endpoint authority; operator adoption follows the documented migrated source outcome.

diagrams.title: A single-use migration lifecycle
diagrams.caption: Unsupported claims or a powered-off source refuse admission. Failure cleanup must preserve safe ownership; success adopts the exact target.

diagrams.title: A user action across two authorization layers
diagrams.caption: Workload mTLS identifies service peers; the stored user token and VM role authorize the action. Manager then controls private QMP through a bounded local API.

diagrams.title: The authenticated graphical console chain
diagrams.caption: Console access is admin-scoped. Private VNC is reached through the manager control socket, BMC admission and exact-VM authenticated proxy hops.

diagrams.title: A guest identity is not the manager identity
diagrams.caption: The optional guest SPIRE agent uses VM-bound software-TPM credentials. The relay carries opaque agent/server TLS bytes and does not issue identities.

diagrams.title: Deletion, retention and destruction have different owners
diagrams.caption: A VM may collect only its proven owned resources. Manual/foreign/unproven state stays retained, and backing bytes follow a separate storage reclaim contract.

diagrams.title: Admit capacity before QEMU hotplug
diagrams.caption: Kubelet Applied describes container resources; manager checks effective cgroups before QMP growth. Guest CPU/memory onlining remains a separate step.

diagrams.title: Which outage affects which operation
diagrams.caption: These are architectural expectations, not availability guarantees. Established kernel resources can outlive their daemon; new changes still need their control-plane owners.

diagrams.title: Source, images and rollout are separate operations
diagrams.caption: A validated source merge does not publish images or deploy a cluster. Release and live verification remain separately authorized steps.

diagrams.title: A digest does not authenticate extra image dependencies
diagrams.caption: The image source digest covers one downloaded file. Backing-file and external-data declarations must be refused before parsing/conversion can select extra inputs. QEMU still owns full image-format validation.

diagrams.title: Desired state and a VM action are different paths
diagrams.caption: A spec change is reconciled through Kubernetes. A bounded Redfish action reaches local QMP/QGA through the manager; powering off in place is not equivalent to deleting the Pod.

diagrams.title: Endpoint authority during a live move
diagrams.caption: The target is prepared but fenced. Activation/source standby occurs in the final pause, followed by adoption and a routing/forwarding grace period. This is a conceptual ownership model, not a new API enum or guarantee for every failure.

diagrams.title: Service admission and user authorization are both required
diagrams.caption: Exact workload identity admits the calling service. The user credential and VM role independently authorize management. This diagram excludes standalone development/alternative native credential entrypoints.

diagrams.title: Local attachment authority starts with a real Pod hierarchy
diagrams.caption: A kernel peer PID is mapped through a validated host unified cgroup and the API-owned Pod to its own VM/NIC. An arbitrary host scope with a Pod-looking UUID does not establish authority. This omits process-lifetime and FD-transfer implementation details.

diagrams.title: Bind process authority through resource use
diagrams.caption: Socket-caller identity and anchor-resource selection are separate checks. The original connector pidfd, held proc directories and opened namespace/file descriptors prevent a later numeric PID/path from substituting another resource. API ownership and own-NIC authorization remain required.

diagrams.title: Same Pod UID, new network namespace
diagrams.caption: The node helper prepares a new namespace generation and manager releases the old backend before requesting fresh queues. Recovery requires guest hot-unplug cooperation; a netd restart observing the same namespace retains its token.

diagrams.title: A bounded control frame carries kernel resources
diagrams.caption: Unix stream fragmentation and SCM_RIGHTS ownership are independent. Every installed descriptor is owned before parse or truncation refusal. The stream grants queues; it does not relay guest packets.

diagrams.title: Linked code and runtime ownership are different maps
diagrams.caption: Selected dependency and runtime relationships. A shared Rust control type is not another service and does not grant a management service ownership of private QMP. This is not a complete dependency/deployment graph.

diagrams.title: Four different kinds of evidence
diagrams.caption: Source, manifest, local real-peer fixture and named live observation answer different questions. Desired state and the user-supplied OpenStack baseline remain separately labeled. No progression to deployed acceptance is implied.

diagrams.title: Current container identity selects the held resource
diagrams.caption: A still-live older same-UID process is not the current anchor container. The API-observed running container, trusted direct cgroup and held process/namespace resources must agree. Same-namespace process refresh preserves the attachment token; unresolved startup waits.

diagrams.title: Desired input, applied generation and late completion
diagrams.caption: A captured byte snapshot supplies both parsed plan and fingerprint. Dependent renewal uses the successful applied generation, and late results cannot replace another local generation. This does not imply a transaction across kernel, provider and API, or make the digest a credential.

diagrams.title: Authenticate requester and local tool provider separately
diagrams.caption: Network peer admission does not authenticate a local tool namespace. The protected Cilium socket original peer and held resource handles select that provider. Private fixtures exercise the binding and namespace transition without changing live BPF maps.

diagrams.title: Verify the owner and pin the endpoint attachment
diagrams.caption: The name locates a resource, exact labels establish own-VM/NIC ownership, and unique CNI attachment identity selects the effect. Name rebinding cannot retarget the PATCH. This is a local API contract, not a live migration/traffic outcome.

diagrams.title: Translate the task, owner and outcome
diagrams.caption: Three daily tasks mapped to their narrower target owners and observable outcomes. The mapping does not imply OpenStack API compatibility or a general automatic evacuation product.

diagrams.title: One workload moves between two clusters
diagrams.caption: A workload-specific cold cutover story: isolated rehearsal, consistency, one writer, final transfer, network authority and acceptance. No OpenStack-to-qrab live migration or storage backend is assumed.

diagrams.title: Rollback changes after target writes
diagrams.caption: The retained source becomes stale after the target accepts writes. Later failback must reconcile data and authority; restarting the old VM alone is not a sufficient procedure.

diagrams.title: Guest identity cleanup has a bounded wait
diagrams.caption: The guest-identity finalizer removes owned entries, optionally stops Pods and calls the scoped evictor, and can release with a Warning after 600 seconds. Other finalizers and previously issued credential lifetimes remain separate.

diagrams.title: A restore needs more than disk bytes
diagrams.caption: A complete workload recovery procedure coordinates data, boot identity, VM intent, network authority, credentials and ownership. Individual primitives exist; the full backup/restore product and measured RTO/RPO are not established.

diagrams.title: Move one workload, then retire its old owner
diagrams.caption: A slide-sized desired cutover: isolated rehearsal, final consistent data, one target/network authority and explicit retention/failback. The accepted-write boundary changes rollback; no performed transfer is implied.

diagrams.title: Different authorities have different revocation clocks
diagrams.caption: A slide-sized continuity view separates human sessions, workload/guest SVIDs, disk writer authority and retained copies. Each needs its own validation, expiry, fencing or destruction evidence.

diagrams.title: Credential cleanup binds the intended VM and Secret
diagrams.caption: A test-only metadata patch checks the intended VM/disk without reading Secret data. Conditional deletion carries the checked object UID/version, so a colliding name, replacement or rotation cannot authorize the wrong cleanup.

diagrams.title: Observed local KVM/container boundary
diagrams.status: dated local fixture / not cluster certification
diagrams.caption: An explicit KVM fixture observes manager PID1 and direct QEMU/swtpm children in one bounded rootless-container cgroup, guest boot/ping and clean original-process exit. It does not establish Kubernetes placement, guest networking or storage-backend acceptance.

diagrams.title: Budget whole memory-device blocks before QMP
diagrams.status: implemented boundary repair / source and wire evidence
diagrams.caption: A one-MiB residual budget cannot authorize a two-MiB device block. The manager now budgets actual whole blocks and reports the true requested size; exact unrepresentable increments use controlled restart. Values illustrate the regression, rather than deployed workload sizing.

diagrams.title: Bind boot-media validation to the actual path
diagrams.caption: A disposable CLI check demonstrates how conflicting roots validated a namesake instead of the actual boot path. The repaired check requires a matching canonical image path. Standard operator roots already match; immutable trusted publication remains part of the contract.

diagrams.title: Separate VM, API, workload and platform authority
diagrams.caption: Four actors use different entrypoints and grants. The dashboard backend is an API actor under its ServiceAccount; an end-user VM role, a workload SVID and platform administration do not collapse into one credential.

diagrams.title: Current and possible tenancy models
diagrams.caption: The current protected-platform foundation differs from a complete tenant-facing VM API and from arbitrary hostile Pod writers. The latter models require explicit policy and isolation work; this is a scope comparison, not a new implemented product.

diagrams.title: Forwarding grace follows the latest handoff
diagrams.caption: A fresh forwarding change resets previous orphan age and shares the sweep lock through its kernel effect. The explicit kernel fixture preserves a replacement, then expires it under its own age. No live Cilium/BGP route outcome is implied.

diagrams.title: Delayed status belongs to its observed object
diagrams.caption: Provider work can outlive a profile name or version. The result is published only with the observed UID/resourceVersion, preserving current status on conflict. Secret ownership and kernel application remain separate operations.

diagrams.title: Image import: names are lookup keys
diagrams.caption: The BaseImage UID/generation scopes Job ownership, report Pods, conditional cleanup and status/finalizer progress. Stage Secret ownership is tested without credential readback. Durable backend adoption remains separate from Kubernetes object ownership.

diagrams.title: Direct QEMU management has four contracts
diagrams.caption: Direct QEMU management separates protocol libraries, manager supervision, Kubernetes/operator workflow and separately owned network/storage/identity capabilities. Their responsibility boundaries remain explicit when libvirt/Nova leave the target.

diagrams.title: Three command outcomes, three next steps
diagrams.caption: Local refusal before dispatch means this request was not sent. A deadline or connection loss after dispatch may leave the remote outcome unknown; the transport does not transparently replay mutations. Wider lifecycle observation and operation-specific retry belong to runtime logic.

diagrams.title: A published target remains the current owner
diagrams.status: implemented repair / private controller API proof
diagrams.caption: VM status records the exact adopted target before a separate Migration completion write. Retry finishes that receipt and retains current Pod/anchors/state/config; owner checks and conditional child effects also apply to refusal and cleanup. This is operator API evidence, not a runtime/storage transaction.
